title: Goodbye, My Friend

jokes.text: Thanks for coming out! Thanks for watching! Love, peace, and hair grease!
jokes.setup: Generic celebrity sign-off phrases building to a conclusion
jokes.punchline: 'Love, peace, and hair grease!' — an absurdly specific, quasi-rhyming sign-off that sounds like a toddler completing a pattern
jokes.explanation: Tracy's random, confidently-delivered non-sequitur perfectly introduces his character in one line. 'Hair grease' is unexpected enough to get a genuine laugh, and it's 100% Tracy-specific. Economy is excellent — three short phrases, escalating absurdity.

jokes.text: Hey, Liz. Me, Lutz, Toofer, and Josh are going to go to that bar where the waiters are dressed like ninjas. You in?
jokes.setup: Frank casually invites Liz out for a Friday night
jokes.punchline: The destination is a bar where waiters are dressed like ninjas — delivered as if this is a completely normal and appealing option
jokes.explanation: Solid 30 Rock texture-comedy. The specificity of 'waiters dressed like ninjas' is funnier than a generic bar, and the casual delivery amplifies the absurdity. It's background worldbuilding humor rather than a major laugh.

jokes.text: Donuts and then bed. What are you depressed about or celebrating?
jokes.setup: Liz is eating donuts late on a Friday night
jokes.punchline: Pete treats 'depressed OR celebrating' as the only two possible explanations for donuts — not bothering to distinguish between them as if they're equivalent
jokes.explanation: Economical and perceptive. The joke is that depression and celebration are treated as functionally identical triggers for donut consumption — very Liz Lemon. Good character integration for both characters; Pete's weary familiarity with Liz is implicit.

jokes.text: How could you cut 'Diaper Chicken'?
jokes.setup: Jenna storms in upset about something being cut from the show
jokes.punchline: The thing cut is called 'Diaper Chicken' — a show-within-a-show sketch name that is pure absurdity
jokes.explanation: The name 'Diaper Chicken' is doing a lot of work in two words. It implies a disgusting, juvenile sketch that Jenna is furious about losing — which tells you everything about her priorities. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: Oh, brother. She's feeling neglected. How's she going to act out this time? My ankle!
jokes.setup: Pete predicts Jenna will act out, mid-sentence
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately fakes an ankle injury — so fast she interrupts Pete's own prediction, collapsing setup and punchline into one moment
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: Pete's prediction IS the setup and Jenna fulfills it before he finishes. The interruption timing makes this land harder than either element alone. Strong character integration — this is pure Jenna.

jokes.text: Oh, 'Imaginary injury.' I would have said 'death of a voice coach.'
jokes.setup: Jenna fakes an ankle injury; Pete and another character react
jokes.punchline: Pete casually names a taxonomy of Jenna's attention-seeking tactics, suggesting these events are so frequent they've developed an internal classification system
jokes.explanation: The implicit gag — that Pete and someone else have mentally catalogued Jenna's antics into a running taxonomy — is rich worldbuilding delivered in one deadpan line. 'Death of a voice coach' as an alternative is a perfect dark comedy detail.

jokes.text: Well, don't you have some gallery opening or a fundraiser to give bow ties to inner city youths?
jokes.setup: Jack says he needs something to do on a Friday night
jokes.punchline: Liz rattles off the most specific, class-coded Jack-activities imaginable — 'bow ties to inner city youths' encapsulates Jack's patrician philanthropy perfectly
jokes.explanation: 'Bow ties to inner city youths' is the perfect satirical distillation of Jack's brand of noblesse oblige. Liz's casual delivery and the escalating specificity of two options makes it feel authentic to her character. High character integration for both.

jokes.text: But I'm committed to Elisa. While she's away, I'm trying to avoid temptation. I just need somewhere I can socialize where women aren't an issue.
jokes.setup: Jack explains why he wants to hang out with the male writers on a Friday night
jokes.punchline: He frames the writers' room as a safe space from women — implying these men are so unattractive/lame that no temptation could occur there
jokes.explanation: The implicit insult to the writers is the joke — Jack doesn't say it directly but the implication is clear. Decent character comedy but the punchline requires the audience to do a bit of work to fully land.

jokes.text: Yeah, Let's go. Hey, now. [Jack walks into the gay bar — reaction beat as everyone turns]
jokes.setup: Jack says he wants to socialize where 'women aren't an issue'; they go to a bar
jokes.punchline: The bar turns out to be a gay bar — fulfilling Jack's stated requirement literally while completely subverting his intent
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock structural joke: the setup contains the punchline if you listen carefully. 'Somewhere women aren't an issue' is immediately literalized. The reaction beat (Jack entering, presumably being greeted enthusiastically) completes the visual joke perfectly. Rewatch bonus for catching the planted logic.

jokes.text: Dude, I know you're getting these messages because I know how to check your voice mail. You are officially a 'D-bag', Tim. I hope you lose your indoor soccer game.
jokes.setup: A teenage girl is leaving an angry voicemail to her ex-boyfriend Tim at the donut shop
jokes.punchline: Her most cutting insult is 'I hope you lose your indoor soccer game' — the most petty, small-scale curse possible from someone who seems to think it's devastating
jokes.explanation: Sharp generational comedy. The combination of tech-savvy menace ('I know how to check your voicemail') with the utterly toothless curse ('I hope you lose your indoor soccer game') creates a perfect portrait of teen melodrama. The specificity of 'indoor soccer' is what elevates it.

jokes.text: Should you be working the night shift alone like this? It's fine. They gave me a gun.
jokes.setup: Liz expresses concern about a teenage girl working the donut night shift alone
jokes.punchline: 'They gave me a gun' — a completely deadpan response that treats workplace-issued firearms as a routine teen employment perk
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan economy. 'They gave me a gun' lands because it's delivered as pure reassurance — the gun is meant to make Liz feel better. Dark subversive in that arming a teenager at a donut shop is presented as responsible management.

jokes.text: You want a dozen donuts to stay? And a skim milk.
jokes.setup: Liz orders a dozen donuts to eat at the shop, then adds 'and a skim milk'
jokes.punchline: The skim milk is the self-deceiving health gesture that cancels absolutely nothing — a perfect Liz Lemon detail
jokes.explanation: Pure Liz Lemon character comedy. The skim milk is the perfect self-deception detail that needs no explanation — it speaks volumes about the character with maximum economy. High character integration.

jokes.text: I don't like that you have crazy-eyes. Oh, shut up, mouth.
jokes.setup: Liz talks to herself about approaching the stranger
jokes.punchline: Liz argues with her own mouth — naming her internal conflict as a dialogue between body parts, telling her mouth to shut up
jokes.explanation: Liz Lemon's social anxieties externalized as a literal argument between her internal voices. 'Shut up, mouth' has a nice absurdist ring. The self-referential body-part attribution is a small but effective bit of character comedy.

jokes.text: What do your dads tell their friends you do? Surgeon. Optometrist. Died. I never really knew my dad, so I just lie to myself. Space assassin.
jokes.setup: Jack asks what the writers' fathers tell people their sons do for a living
jokes.punchline: The answers escalate — 'Surgeon,' 'Optometrist' (respectable lies), then 'Died' (father says the son died rather than admit he writes comedy), then the kicker: 'I lie to myself. Space assassin.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation structure is textbook perfect: two plausible lies (surgeon, optometrist), then a dark leap ('Died' — the father would rather his son be dead than a comedy writer), then a final absurdist gut-punch ('Space assassin'). Each beat tops the last. 'Died' alone is a 7; 'Space assassin' as the self-lie pushes it to 9. The joke simultaneously roasts the writers' room and builds character. Highly quotable, rewards rewatching to catch the escalation beats.

jokes.text: In Sicilian dialect, it means 'well poisoner.' In Gaelic, Donaghy means 'dung basket.'
jokes.setup: Frank talks about restoring the glory of the Rossitano name
jokes.punchline: The name means 'well poisoner' in Sicilian; Jack's name means 'dung basket' in Gaelic — both men have surnames that are actively embarrassing
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure works well — both men share the joke's humiliation equally. 'Dung basket' is funnier than 'well poisoner' because it's lower-stakes gross, and applying it to the patrician Jack Donaghy is ideal. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Last time I saw my dad, he went out to get the candles for my fourth birthday lasagna and never came back.
jokes.setup: Frank shares the story of his father abandoning the family
jokes.punchline: 'Birthday lasagna' — the dark abandonment story is undercut by the absurdity of 'lasagna' replacing 'cake,' making it simultaneously sadder and funnier
jokes.explanation: 'Birthday lasagna' is a perfect 30 Rock micro-joke embedded in an otherwise earnest story. It does double duty: it makes Frank more specific and Italian-American, and it generates a laugh precisely where the story should be devastating. The specificity (candles for a lasagna) is what makes it work.

jokes.text: We're going to Lutz's to watch movies. Tonight, a classic. Harry and the Hendersons. You in, Jack? Uh, yes. But I don't want to go to Lutz's apartment. His contract is up, and I don't want to feel sorry for him.
jokes.setup: Jack is invited to watch Harry and the Hendersons at Lutz's apartment
jokes.punchline: Jack refuses to go to Lutz's apartment because 'his contract is up and I don't want to feel sorry for him' — treating the impending firing of a human being as a personal inconvenience to Jack's emotional comfort
jokes.explanation: Jack's sociopathic brand of emotional management is perfectly captured: he's not heartless, he just doesn't want to be inconvenienced by guilt. The matter-of-fact delivery makes it land. High character integration.

jokes.text: When I was your age, you could just be like, 'Oh, he probably tried to call me, but my line was busy.' And then just... watch Falcon Crest and cry yourself to sleep.
jokes.setup: Liz and Becca bond over guys using technology to avoid calling
jokes.punchline: Liz's version of coping is a specific '80s/'90s callback — 'busy signal' plausible deniability + Falcon Crest + crying. The specificity of 'Falcon Crest' as the sob-show of choice is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Liz Lemon — self-deprecating, era-specific, and sad in a way that's also funny. 'Falcon Crest' is a specific enough reference to reward viewers who know it while being funny as a cultural artifact regardless. High character integration.

jokes.text: They all seemed really old and weird. Not one of them even knew who Ne-Yo is.
jokes.setup: Becca describes why she hasn't found a suitable adoptive parent
jokes.punchline: Her criteria for a good parent includes knowing who Ne-Yo is — a teen's deeply skewed prioritization of what matters in a parent
jokes.explanation: Good generational gap joke. Becca's criteria for parenthood being 'knows Ne-Yo' is a pointed commentary on teen priorities. Sets up the next joke perfectly.

jokes.text: # I need you... / Finally! Thank you! Somebody cool, for once.
jokes.setup: Liz hums/sings Ne-Yo to herself; Becca has just said she needs adoptive parents who know Ne-Yo
jokes.punchline: Becca immediately seizes on Liz as a cool adult — the joke is that Liz knowing Ne-Yo (however superficially) is enough to qualify her as a great potential parent in Becca's eyes
jokes.explanation: Quick and structurally clean callback. The instant qualification of Liz as a 'cool' adult solely on Ne-Yo recognition is both flattering and absurd. The joke works on the irony that Liz — who we know is a mess — passes this very low bar with flying colors.

jokes.text: Get out of here! Can't you see we don't want you anymore? Why can't you go back where you came from? And leave us alone! Go. Go!
jokes.setup: Emotional dialogue that sounds like it could be directed at a person being cruelly rejected
jokes.punchline: Revealed to be from Harry and the Hendersons — a man yelling at Bigfoot, not a person — recontextualizing the cruel-sounding words entirely
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection. The audience hears cruel rejection dialogue; the reveal that it's from a Bigfoot movie recontextualizes everything. This also plants the thematic setup that will pay off in the Frank storyline and Liz-Becca storyline later. Rewatch bonus for the foreshadowing.

jokes.text: Goodbye, my friend. He had to be mean to save him. Harry belonged in the woods.
jokes.setup: Jack and Frank watch Harry and the Hendersons; George Henderson drives Harry away
jokes.punchline: Two grown professional men (one a corporate titan) are deeply, earnestly moved by a 1987 Bigfoot family comedy
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes entirely from the gap between these characters' status/intelligence and their genuine emotional investment in Harry and the Hendersons. The deadpan delivery of 'Harry belonged in the woods' as sincere film analysis is perfect.

jokes.text: This reminds me of my favorite movie. Shane. Oh! When Joey wants to go with Shane and Shane makes him stay. Maybe it's because we didn't have fathers. Maybe that's why we're drawn to movies where the father figure pushes away the child/legendary North American forest ape.
jokes.setup: Frank and Jack bond over their shared emotional response to Harry and the Hendersons
jokes.punchline: Jack's psychoanalytic summary classifies Bigfoot as a 'legendary North American forest ape' in the same category as children of absent fathers — the clinical descriptor is the joke
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The phrase 'child/legendary North American forest ape' is doing tremendous work — it's Jack's corporate/clinical vocabulary applied to an absurd emotional truth. The psychological insight (absent fathers → father-figure movies) is real and then completely derailed by the Bigfoot qualifier. Jack Donaghy specifically would say this. Highly quotable, strong structure.

jokes.text: I don't have a birthday, Ken. What? I don't have a birth certificate because I was born inside of Yankee Stadium.
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Tracy for his birthday for the staff list
jokes.punchline: Tracy doesn't have a birthday because he was born inside Yankee Stadium — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is a normal and sufficient explanation
jokes.explanation: Peak Tracy Jordan mythology-building. The Yankee Stadium birth story is absurd enough to be funny on its face, and Tracy's sincere matter-of-fact delivery is everything. High character integration — only Tracy could have this backstory and deliver it this way.

jokes.text: Oh, but even prisoners have birthday parties. I saw one on Oz. It was... interesting.
jokes.setup: Kenneth tries to comfort Tracy by noting everyone has birthdays
jokes.punchline: 'I saw one on Oz. It was... interesting.' — The ellipsis implies Kenneth witnessed something very specifically traumatic in the HBO prison drama, expressed with his characteristic wholesome understatement
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's innocence colliding with the brutality of HBO's Oz is perfectly rendered in the loaded pause before 'interesting.' The joke trusts the audience to fill in what a Oz birthday party would entail. This is top-tier Kenneth characterization — his unwavering positivity cracking ever so slightly. High craft.

jokes.text: And because of my drinking, they're often a surprise.
jokes.setup: Kenneth describes birthday parties as events where you're 'surrounded by people who love you'
jokes.punchline: Tracy adds that his parties are often 'a surprise' because of his drinking — meaning he's too blackout drunk to know they're happening
jokes.explanation: Beautiful subversion of 'surprise party.' Tracy flips the meaning: the surprise isn't that guests show up unexpectedly — it's that he's too drunk to be conscious of reality. Delivered flatly as a positive feature of the situation. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: My birthday's September 21st. Not that anyone asked.
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Tracy are discussing Tracy's lack of a birthday
jokes.punchline: Jenna interjects with her birthday — which nobody asked about — establishing that she's been listening jealously and is already angling for attention
jokes.explanation: A small but efficient Jenna joke. 'Not that anyone asked' is doing all the character work — she's simultaneously fishing for attention and acknowledging no one cares. The timing (mid-conversation about someone else) is perfect character integration.

jokes.text: This morning it hit me in the shower why the Hendersons named their guest 'Harry.' That film has layers.
jokes.setup: Jack brings up his overnight reflection on Harry and the Hendersons
jokes.punchline: Jack spent the night intellectually working out that 'Harry' = 'hairy' (for Bigfoot) and presents this like a profound cinematic discovery: 'That film has layers.'
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. Jack Donaghy — a man of extraordinary intelligence and resources — spent the night in profound reflection and arrived at 'Harry = hairy.' The punchline is that Jack presents this obvious wordplay as a sophisticated revelation, capped with 'That film has layers.' It's a perfect distillation of how overqualified people apply their intellect to trivial things. The character integration is flawless — only Jack would deliver this with complete sincerity and authority.

jokes.text: We both have recurring dreams about being overpowered by a female bodybuilder.
jokes.setup: Jack is listing the things he and Frank have in common as he tries to bond with him
jokes.punchline: The shared trait is a very specific recurring dream involving a female bodybuilder — delivered without hesitation as if this is as unremarkable as sharing a hobby
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The specificity ('recurring,' 'female bodybuilder,' 'overpowered') and Jack's casual delivery make this land hard. It's absurd but delivered with Jack's characteristic authority, which makes it funnier. The fact that Frank doesn't deny it is the perfect button. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Make your mother proud, Frank. Make your father hate any new children he might have.
jokes.setup: Jack offers Frank a full scholarship to Columbia Law and says 'make your mother proud'
jokes.punchline: He adds 'Make your father hate any new children he might have' — a specific, targeted wish for revenge against an absent father's potential replacement family
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The first half ('make your mother proud') is the expected motivational line; the second half pirouettes into targeted, specific, deeply personal revenge fantasy against a man with a replacement family. 'Any new children he might have' is the perfect qualifier — it's not just the father Jack wants hurt, it's the idea of a new family the father chose over Frank. This is Jack Donaghy at his most unhinged-but-sincere. Among the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: But we both know you shouldn't be working at a desk with... fake vomit on it. Right. Fake.
jokes.setup: Jack gestures at Frank's desk prop/toy — fake vomit — to illustrate that Frank has outgrown his environment
jokes.punchline: 'Right. Fake.' — Frank's pause and deadpan confirmation implies the vomit might not be fake, or at least that the distinction requires acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: A gem of economy. Jack's slight pause before 'fake' followed by Frank's barely-there confirmation 'Right. Fake.' creates the exact right ambiguity. The visual gag (actual vomit/prop vomit on a comedy writer's desk) and the deadpan exchange are perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Oh, God. Please don't be a daughter I didn't know about.
jokes.setup: Jack is interrupted by someone entering unexpectedly
jokes.punchline: Jack's first thought is that it might be a secret daughter — which implies this is a recurring realistic fear for him, not an extreme scenario
jokes.explanation: The joke is that this fear is plausible for Jack — he's lived the kind of life where an unknown daughter is a real possibility. The prayer-like 'Oh, God' adds to the comedy. Good character integration.

jokes.text: So, do you want me to start Youth Consulting now? Because kids would not be into that.
jokes.setup: Becca sees the TGS workplace and offers her perspective as a teenager
jokes.punchline: Her instinct is to immediately consult on what kids want — and her first note is that whatever she just witnessed 'kids would not be into'
jokes.explanation: A decent character joke that works on the implicit absurdity of TGS employing a pregnant teenager as a 'youth consultant.' Her immediate critical assessment is funny but not particularly surprising.

jokes.text: Oh! That's horrible. My heart goes out to all the inner city kids. Especially those too fat to dance their way out.
jokes.setup: Kenneth tells Jenna that Tracy has never had a birthday party
jokes.punchline: Jenna pivots from Tracy's specific situation to a general statement of compassion — immediately undermined by 'especially those too fat to dance their way out,' which reveals her 'compassion' is both reductive and insulting
jokes.explanation: Jenna's faux-compassion reveals itself in the qualifier — she believes the only escape from inner-city poverty is dancing talent, and she's expressing pity for those physically unable to perform that escape. It's a perfect encapsulation of celebrity obliviousness. The pivot from Tracy to 'all inner city kids' is also a great character beat.

jokes.text: I'm glad you feel that way. Because we have this big party planned for you. I know! And we thought you could share it with Mr. Jordan! [pause] Isn't that a great idea? [pause] That's so great!
jokes.setup: Kenneth reveals that Jenna's birthday party will be shared with Tracy
jokes.punchline: Jenna's visible horror is followed by her forced, hollow 'That's so great!' — the gap between the reaction beats and her final answer tells you everything
jokes.explanation: The pregnant pauses ('Isn't that a great idea?') are doing the comedy work here — Jenna's reaction is presumably visible horror, and Kenneth is presumably either oblivious or just pushing through it. The cringe builds through the double-beat silence before her forced acceptance.

jokes.text: # Now, we are joined / in a cobweb of rainbows...? Stop. Tears. The world needs to hear your music.
jokes.setup: Becca plays Liz one of her songs — which is clearly terrible
jokes.punchline: Liz's response ('Tears. The world needs to hear your music.') is delivered as either genuine emotion or a magnificent lie — implying the song was so bad it caused tears, but Liz is deciding to be encouraging anyway
jokes.explanation: 'Cobweb of rainbows' is a deliberately terrible lyric, and Liz's one-word reaction ('Tears') is ambiguous — it could be aesthetic horror or genuine emotion. The ambiguity is the joke. 'The world needs to hear your music' as a response to this lyric is the episode's most elaborate lie.

jokes.text: Being terrible has never prevented success in the music business. Look at Biz Markie or The Doors.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to defend encouraging Becca's music; Pete objects
jokes.punchline: Pete's examples of terrible-but-successful artists are Biz Markie (fair game) and The Doors (a genuinely beloved band, included as if they're obviously terrible)
jokes.explanation: Biz Markie is the safe example; The Doors is the provocation. Pete casually grouping Jim Morrison's legacy with Biz Markie is the joke — it's a strong opinion delivered as obvious fact. Works as both a comedy writing room character beat and a standalone observational joke.

jokes.text: And when my caveman brain saw those babies with their little Hornberger foreheads... it clicked.
jokes.setup: Pete describes his experience of becoming a father despite initial terror
jokes.punchline: 'Hornberger foreheads' — Pete's babies are lovable specifically because of a genetic trait specific to his family, delivered as both a term of endearment and a slightly alarming physical description
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Hornberger foreheads' is what makes this work. It implies Pete's family has a notably large/distinctive forehead, and that seeing this trait on his newborns triggered paternal love. 'Caveman brain' is also a nice touch — Pete's self-awareness about his own primitive rewiring.

jokes.text: My pregnant teen message board says the baby gets all its food from the mother. So, you have to give it stuff it likes.
jokes.setup: Becca is giving Liz nutritional advice based on an online pregnancy forum
jokes.punchline: The advice — that a fetus gets food it 'likes' directly from what the mother eats — is complete medical nonsense, treated as authoritative sourced information from 'my pregnant teen message board'
jokes.explanation: 'My pregnant teen message board' as a medical authority is a sharp satirical detail. The misinformation about fetal nutrition delivered with total confidence captures a very specific kind of teen online culture.

jokes.text: I'm going to post a reply to Juno 32 and tell her she's a giant ass wipe.
jokes.setup: Liz corrects Becca's medical misinformation about fetal nutrition
jokes.punchline: Rather than accepting the correction, Becca's instinct is to attack the original source on the message board — and the username 'Juno 32' is a perfect 2009 joke (referencing the then-recent film, implying teen pregnancy internet culture)
jokes.explanation: 'Juno 32' is a brilliant detail — it implies there are at least 31 other Junos on this message board, suggesting the cultural saturation of the film. Becca turning her anger outward at a stranger rather than accepting correction is perfect character work.

jokes.text: You already dress like a mom. ...And stop.
jokes.setup: Becca compliments Liz — 'you're smart, successful, grounded...' — and Liz says 'Oh... go on.' Then Becca adds: 'You already dress like a mom.'
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately shuts down the compliment parade with '...And stop.' — the one thing she doesn't want to hear is that her wardrobe screams 'mom'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. The compliment escalation ('smart, successful, grounded') pulls Liz in with 'oh, go on'; the pivot to 'you dress like a mom' lands hard because it's both a compliment in this context and an insult in Liz's. Her '...And stop' is the perfect button — economical, in character, and highly quotable. One of the episode's best exchanges.

jokes.text: # Mothers and fathers and jugglers and judges... # Now, we are joined in a cobweb of rainbows...
jokes.setup: The emotional moment between Liz and Becca culminates in them singing together
jokes.punchline: They sing Becca's terrible song ('mothers and fathers and jugglers and judges' — 'jugglers' being the absurd non sequitur in an otherwise earnest list) together with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: The callback to the terrible song works because 'jugglers' is now in the lyrics alongside 'judges' — the song is getting worse on repeat exposure. The visual of Liz earnestly singing along to this is the real joke.

jokes.text: What a schmo, entering first. Now, I'm the headliner, and he's just the warm-up act. I'm Mr. Don Rickles and he's just me.
jokes.setup: Tracy accidentally enters the surprise birthday party first, stealing Jenna's thunder
jokes.punchline: 'I'm Mr. Don Rickles and he's just me.' — Jenna's analogy breaks down completely in real time; she casts herself as Don Rickles and Tracy as 'just me' (Jenna), which means Tracy is the star and Jenna is... Jenna
jokes.explanation: This joke rewards attention. Jenna's analogy — meant to establish her superiority — accidentally confirms that 'being just Jenna' is the lesser position. She casts herself as Don Rickles without realizing the analogy means Tracy is her and she's stuck as his opening act. The self-defeating structure is perfectly Jenna. Rewatch bonus: the logical collapse is funnier each time.

jokes.text: And to think I was just calling y'all a bunch of racists. Aw... Stop... Jenna time.
jokes.setup: Tracy is moved by his surprise birthday party and tells his coworkers he loves them
jokes.punchline: He immediately segues from 'I love you all' to 'I was calling y'all a bunch of racists' — implying this was his normal operating assumption before this moment; then Jenna cuts in with 'Jenna time' to redirect attention
jokes.explanation: 'Racist' as Tracy's default assumption about his coworkers, casually dropped in the middle of a heartfelt moment, is sharp dark comedy. 'Jenna time' as her method of claiming space at any emotionally charged moment is perfect Jenna shorthand.

jokes.text: Jenna time. / Friends. I am leaving T.G.S. for Columbia Law School—
jokes.setup: Jenna tries to reclaim the spotlight at Tracy's birthday by calling 'Jenna time'
jokes.punchline: Instead of Jenna's speech, Frank hijacks the moment to announce he's going to law school — completely stealing Jenna's spotlight with something completely unrelated
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — 'Jenna time' is established as something she calls, then the setup is immediately stolen. Works as misdirection and character comedy simultaneously.

jokes.text: I am leaving T.G.S. for Columbia Law School to pursue my dream of becoming a lawyer. [long pause / shocked silence]
jokes.setup: Frank makes a dramatic announcement at the party
jokes.punchline: The announcement is met with stunned silence — the reaction beat is the joke; no one at TGS can process a writer actually having aspirations
jokes.explanation: The comedy is structural: the announcement is played completely straight in a context (a birthday party) that maximizes its incongruity. The collective silence implies everyone knows this is either delusional or devastating.

jokes.text: Did you know that if you sing 'Happy Birthday' on a TV show, you have to pay for it? I did not know that. # Hap...? Hey!
jokes.setup: Someone begins singing 'Happy Birthday' at the party
jokes.punchline: Jack stops them with a copyright disclaimer — the show fourth-wall-adjacent moment where TGS (and by extension 30 Rock) can't afford to air the song
jokes.explanation: A real-world fact (Happy Birthday copyright) deployed as a gag. The meta quality — a TV show acknowledging TV licensing reality — is clever without being too self-congratulatory. Jack's role as the person who would know and enforce this is perfect.

jokes.text: My dad got us all seats for Opening Day at the new Yankee Stadium! Cerie! Cerie! Cerie!
jokes.setup: People are trying to replace 'Happy Birthday' with an appropriate celebration; Tracy announces something
jokes.punchline: Tracy's birthday wish/announcement pivots to his father getting Opening Day seats at the new Yankee Stadium — which the crowd goes absolutely insane for, chanting 'Cerie!' (apparently Cerie is involved somehow, or the crowd is just naming the most exciting person)
jokes.explanation: The crowd's eruption at 'Cerie!' is the absurd punchline — the most unexpected person to be chanted is the intern/receptionist. A decent absurdist beat that plays on the chaos of the birthday party.

jokes.text: Oh. Ow. Cerie! Cerie! / No one ask me about my back brace. / Make a wish, Mr. Jordan. Blow out the candles. / No one ask about my back brace!
jokes.setup: In the midst of the party chaos, Jenna appears in a back brace
jokes.punchline: Jenna insists twice that no one ask about her back brace — while clearly desperate for someone to ask about her back brace
jokes.explanation: A callback to Jenna's attention-seeking injury pattern, but now literalized with a visible prop. 'No one ask about my back brace' repeated twice is the perfect inverse-psychology move — a transparent attempt to generate concern. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Now, let me hear you say the seven most important words in the American Judicial System. My client... has no memory of that. I also would have accepted, 'You can't prove that's the governor's semen.'
jokes.setup: Jack tests Frank on his new legal identity; Frank delivers the first 'seven words'
jokes.punchline: 'You can't prove that's the governor's semen' — Jack's alternative 'most important legal phrase' implies both that this is a common enough legal situation to have a standard phrase AND that Jack has personal familiarity with it
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's very best jokes. 'My client has no memory of that' is solid — a lawyer's standard dodge. But 'You can't prove that's the governor's semen' is an all-timer. It's specific ('governor's' rather than a generic politician), it's darkly implied that this is A REAL THING that has been litigated, and Jack delivers it as if offering a helpful educational alternative. Highly quotable, strong character integration — Jack Donaghy would know this phrase from experience.

jokes.text: You were right, Ken. Birthdays are special. And now, mine is over. And who knows when February 24th will come again? Now, that warm, happy feeling is gone, there's no cake in my mouth, and that birthday wish is malarkey. Malarkey!
jokes.setup: The birthday party is over; Tracy reflects on the experience
jokes.punchline: 'Who knows when February 24th will come again?' — Tracy doesn't understand calendars/time well enough to know that dates repeat annually; 'malarkey' is a perfect vintage-sounding expletive for Tracy to deploy
jokes.explanation: 'Who knows when February 24th will come again' is the key line — it reveals Tracy exists outside normal temporal understanding, which is perfect Tracy mythology. The building despair over 'no cake in my mouth' and 'malarkey' (twice) shows Tracy's emotional intensity applied to the most ordinary things.

jokes.text: Someday, you'll have an ad on the subway in English and Spanish.
jokes.setup: Frank's mother gushes about Frank becoming a lawyer
jokes.punchline: Her ultimate vision of legal success is a subway ad in two languages — not 'partner at a firm' or 'arguing before the Supreme Court,' but a multilingual transit advertisement
jokes.explanation: The subway ad as the pinnacle of professional success is a sharp class-comedy observation. The specificity of 'English and Spanish' implies the market she's imagining (personal injury, immigration law). It's a precise, affectionate portrait of working-class immigrant ambition.

jokes.text: What do you think you're doing to my boy? [...] His father was a lawyer! And his father's father! All the Rossitano men are lawyers. It's in their blood to be lawyers! [...] For the mob!
jokes.setup: Frank's mother confronts Jack for trying to push Frank into law, building to what sounds like a proud family legacy of lawyers
jokes.punchline: 'For the mob!' — the proud legal legacy is mob law; the family doesn't have lawyers who practice law, they practice mob law
jokes.explanation: Textbook misdirection with perfect structural execution. 'All the Rossitano men are lawyers — it's in their blood to be lawyers!' builds to what should be an inspirational reveal. The three-word punchline 'For the mob!' subverts everything perfectly. The pause before it is presumably doing critical comedic work. The setup also recontextualizes 'well poisoner' from earlier.

jokes.text: You want me to paint you a picture? Because I did. It's part of a therapy through painting thing.
jokes.setup: Frank's mom says she could explain the mob danger more vividly
jokes.punchline: She has literally painted the threat — as part of art therapy — and is offering to show Jack the painting as evidence of the danger
jokes.explanation: Taking the idiom literally ('paint you a picture') and then revealing she actually has, through art therapy, is a strong absurdist joke. The therapy angle adds a layer — this woman processes mob-related trauma through painting.

jokes.text: He's coming to steal my baby.
jokes.setup: Liz learns that Tim (Becca's ex-boyfriend/father of the child) has arrived at the building
jokes.punchline: Liz frames the situation as Tim 'stealing her baby' — the baby that isn't hers, from the mother who is also not hers to possess. Liz has completely lost perspective after less than two days.
jokes.explanation: Liz's instantaneous possessive attachment — calling it 'her baby' after two days — is funny and sad simultaneously. The speed of her emotional investment is the joke, and it's perfectly in character for Liz.

jokes.text: Don't even ask about the wheelchair. Okay. Also, my old vocal coach died! Come on, come on...
jokes.setup: Jenna arrives in a wheelchair, having escalated from ankle injury to back brace to full wheelchair
jokes.punchline: 'Also, my old vocal coach died!' — Jenna stacks a completely unrelated tragedy onto her physical injuries in a bid for maximum sympathy, but the 'also' delivery makes it feel like an afterthought
jokes.explanation: A perfect trifecta callback: ankle injury → back brace → wheelchair, and now the 'death of a voice coach' predicted by Pete in act one actually happens. The escalation of Jenna's attention-seeking props AND the callback to Pete's earlier prediction makes this very satisfying. 'Come on, come on' (Jenna seemingly willing someone to ask) is the button.

jokes.text: There was once a great American named George Henderson. He met a woodland ape, or Sasquatch, who, despite its dangerous message of environmentalism, became his friend. But when the time came to do the hard thing and send it back into the forest where it belonged... and birds could perch on its shoulder because it was gentle... George Henderson summoned the strength, and, by God, he did it. Did it hurt? You bet it hurt. Like a bastard. But he did it because it was the right thing to do. For the woodland ape.
jokes.setup: Liz is about to interfere in Becca and Tim's reunion; Jack intercepts her to deliver a speech
jokes.punchline: Jack delivers an elaborate, completely sincere Harry and the Hendersons parable as serious life advice — including 'despite its dangerous message of environmentalism' and 'birds could perch on its shoulder because it was gentle' as earnest qualifiers
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best extended bits. Jack's Harry and the Hendersons speech works on multiple levels: it's his genuine attempt to give meaningful advice using the only emotional vocabulary he's developed (Bigfoot movies); the qualifiers ('dangerous message of environmentalism,' 'birds could perch on its shoulder because it was gentle') show he's thought about this movie deeply and specifically; and 'Like a bastard' as a pain descriptor is beautifully incongruous with the earnest fable register. The callback pays off the entire Harry and the Hendersons setup from the episode's middle section.

jokes.text: I'm the one who's been there for Becca. For almost two days!
jokes.setup: Liz is justifying why she should have a say in Becca's decision
jokes.punchline: 'For almost two days!' — the self-aware underselling of her claim, which she delivers with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The honesty of 'almost two days' is the joke — Liz is so desperate she doesn't even notice how weak her claim is. Delivered with sincerity, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: There was once a great American named George Henderson... despite its dangerous message of environmentalism... and birds could perch on its shoulder because it was gentle...
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to talk Liz out of intervening in Becca's life using Harry and the Hendersons as a metaphor
jokes.punchline: Jack's deadpan description of Harry and the Hendersons includes 'its dangerous message of environmentalism' and 'birds could perch on its shoulder because it was gentle' — treating a children's movie with the gravity of a policy paper
jokes.explanation: Jack Donaghy delivering a policy analysis of Harry and the Hendersons with complete sincerity is extremely funny. 'Dangerous message of environmentalism' is perfect — only Jack would identify environmentalism as dangerous. The 'birds could perch on its shoulder because it was gentle' detail is absurdly specific and sincere.

jokes.text: Is that Harry and the Hendersons? You've seen it? This is my life, Jack.
jokes.setup: Jack finishes his elaborate Bigfoot fable; Liz realizes he's describing a movie
jokes.punchline: 'This is my life, Jack.' — Liz's weariness about the fact that Jack is using a Bigfoot film as the lens through which he views and advises on human experience is the joke
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to Jack's speech. 'This is my life, Jack' — said with complete exhaustion — is both a laugh line and a genuine character moment. Liz Lemon's resigned acceptance of Jack's eccentric life philosophy is perfectly rendered in five words.

jokes.text: Oh my! Miss Maroney, are you okay? Well, I think I'll be okay in time for tomorrow's show. But then, I have to go in for more tests. I'm so brave.
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks about Jenna's back brace
jokes.punchline: 'I'm so brave.' — Jenna's self-assessment of her own bravery, delivered with complete sincerity, is the joke; she's praising herself for enduring what appears to be a fake injury
jokes.explanation: Jenna praising her own bravery for enduring a likely-fabricated injury is quintessential Jenna. The deadpan delivery of 'I'm so brave' as a standalone sentence is an excellent button.

jokes.text: Oh! Miss Maroney, are you okay? Well, I think I'll be okay in time for tomorrow's show. But then, I have to go in for more tests. I'm so brave.
jokes.setup: Kenneth sees Jenna in a wheelchair and expresses concern.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm so brave' — Jenna self-labeling her own bravery in the third person, in a context where her ailments are almost certainly fake.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm so brave' is a great line — self-awarded courage for a manufactured situation. The structure is good: 'I'll be okay for tomorrow's show' (professional) → 'more tests' (escalation) → 'I'm so brave' (narcissistic payoff).

jokes.text: We've narrowed it down to... own a RoboCop, hunt that elephant that paints, or breakfast in bed.
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Jenna try to figure out Tracy's birthday wish so they can extend his birthday
jokes.punchline: The three options for Tracy's wish are: own a RoboCop, hunt the famous elephant that paints, or breakfast in bed — two absurd impossible wishes and one completely ordinary thing
jokes.explanation: Excellent 30 Rock list joke. The structure: absurd (own a RoboCop), escalating absurd with a dark turn (hunt the elephant that paints — implying Tracy wants to kill a famous gentle animal), then the comedic whiplash of 'breakfast in bed' as an equally valid option. The fact that these three are considered equivalent by Kenneth is the real joke. 'Hunt that elephant that paints' specifically is inspired — it's a real cultural reference (famous painting elephants) twisted into something sinister. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: But it wasn't his birthday! It was my birthday! Oh, forget it. I'm tired of making you people try to care for me. You don't care for me, clearly. Nobody does.
jokes.setup: Jenna realizes the birthday party attention has all shifted to Tracy
jokes.punchline: Jenna's dramatic declaration that 'nobody does' (care for her) — a statement of genuine self-pity delivered with theatrical flair — is the joke; she's right AND she's being absurd about it simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Functional Jenna character comedy. The escalation from frustration to existential 'nobody does' is very Jenna, but it's a familiar beat for the character and doesn't do anything new. The delivery likely saves it.

jokes.text: My birthday wish came true! I wished for you to get better. I was going to wish for breakfast in bed with RoboCop while that elephant paints us. We were close.
jokes.setup: Tracy reveals his birthday wish was for Jenna to feel better (touching); then clarifies what he almost wished for instead
jokes.punchline: 'Breakfast in bed with RoboCop while that elephant paints us. We were close.' — The alternative wish combines all three previous elements into one maximally absurd scenario; 'We were close' implies breakfast in bed with RoboCop is almost the same as wishing someone good health
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. Tracy's birthday wish callback takes the three separate absurd options from Kenneth's list and synthesizes them into one unified mega-wish ('breakfast in bed with RoboCop while that elephant paints us'), then delivers 'We were close' as if wishing for Jenna's health and wishing for a RoboCop portrait session are in the same emotional neighborhood. The structure is impeccable — setup, callback, synthesis, and the devastating understatement button. Earned vs. cheap score is a 9 because it required three prior jokes to set up. This is the kind of callback that defines 30 Rock's architecture.

jokes.text: Now, let's make Miss Maroney's birthday wish come true! Oh, that's so sweet. But who would I celebrate with if y'all were in a car accident?
jokes.setup: Tracy offers to help make Jenna's birthday wish come true
jokes.punchline: Jenna's birthday wish apparently involves everyone she knows being in a car accident — implied by her hypothetical worry about who she'd celebrate with if that happened
jokes.explanation: The implication that Jenna's birthday wish involves a mass car accident is wonderfully dark. The phrasing 'who would I celebrate with if y'all were in a car accident' suggests this is a specific scenario she's thought through, not a hypothetical. Perfect dark Jenna comedy.

jokes.text: I'm her friend. Jenna. And she does not want to see you. She's very mad, and she wants you to leave.
jokes.setup: Tim arrives to see Becca; Jenna intercepts him in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Jenna introduces herself as 'her friend. Jenna.' — the name drop as if it should mean something — while relaying Becca's alleged wishes; the joke is that Jenna has appointed herself Becca's spokesperson despite knowing her for approximately one day
jokes.explanation: Jenna's celebrity self-introduction ('her friend. Jenna.') is a decent character beat. The joke that she expects her name to register with a random teenager is understated but works.

jokes.text: Ugh! Fine, Lithgow! I'll do the right thing. God! I guess someone's been watching The World According to Garp. Damn it. Tim, wait.
jokes.setup: Liz is watching what seems to be a John Lithgow movie and arguing with it about doing the right thing
jokes.punchline: Liz addresses John Lithgow directly ('Fine, Lithgow!') as if he's lecturing her; then self-congratulatingly references The World According to Garp before chasing Tim
jokes.explanation: Liz arguing with a Lithgow movie and then immediately citing another Lithgow film as her moral framework is a good character beat. The specificity of Garp as the source of ethical clarity is a nice meta joke — Liz gets her values from '80s literary adaptations.

jokes.text: No, when you said she didn't want to see me, it was such a relief.
jokes.setup: Liz chases Tim to convince him to stay; Tim reacts
jokes.punchline: Tim honestly admits that being told Becca didn't want to see him was a relief — confirming Liz's earlier assessment of him without any self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Tim's honest admission is a decent observational beat about young men and responsibility. Functional comedy that serves the plot more than the laugh track.

jokes.text: Do you love Becca? She's like my soul mate. I mean... You're not listening, dummy!
jokes.setup: Liz asks Tim if he loves Becca; he begins to qualify his answer
jokes.punchline: 'You're not listening, dummy!' — Liz interrupts Tim's own answer to tell him he's not listening, when in fact Tim was in mid-sentence answering the question
jokes.explanation: Liz's controlling, impatient dynamic plays well here. She asked the question but isn't interested in the answer — she already knows what she wants Tim to feel. 'Dummy' has a nice Liz energy.

jokes.text: And get married and have disposable cameras at the wedding because it's fun and people like it. Where are we going? I already cleaned out my office.
jokes.setup: Liz is mid-speech to Tim about getting married; Frank suddenly appears, having cleaned out his office
jokes.punchline: Frank has already acted on Jack's revoked scholarship offer — he's completely cleaned out his office — right as we cut to him appearing behind Liz mid-monologue
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — Frank appears at exactly the wrong moment having done exactly the irreversible thing. 'I already cleaned out my office' as a confused response to 'where are we going?' implies Frank has been marching around with his belongings waiting for someone to direct him.

jokes.text: You've got to go. No. I'm going to be a lawyer. I'm going to be like you. Get out of here! Go to the writers' room! There is no scholarship! Can't you see we don't want you anymore?
jokes.setup: Jack must crush Frank's dreams using the Harry and the Hendersons methodology — being cruel to save him
jokes.punchline: Jack recreates the George Henderson scene ('Can't you see we don't want you anymore?') beat for beat on Frank — the Bigfoot fable becomes the literal script for the confrontation
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the episode's Harry and the Hendersons throughline. Jack doesn't just use the movie as a metaphor — he literally performs it on Frank. 'Can't you see we don't want you anymore?' echoes the movie dialogue from act one verbatim. The rewatch bonus is significant: knowing the movie dialogue from the earlier scene makes this land much harder. The episode's thematic architecture is visible here — this is exactly what well-crafted sitcom plotting looks like.

jokes.text: Goodbye, my friend. [Beat] [Jack watches Frank go]
jokes.setup: Frank has left; Jack watches from a window — mirroring the Harry and the Hendersons scene
jokes.punchline: The episode title delivered as a straight line in a moment that is simultaneously genuinely touching and absurd because it's about Frank
jokes.explanation: The episode title as the button to the Frank/Jack storyline, delivered sincerely, is beautifully economical. The entire Harry and the Hendersons subplot pays off here — Jack genuinely sees himself as George Henderson saying goodbye to the forest ape. The comedy lives in the sincerity applied to an absurd situation.

jokes.text: Hey, baby. My God. Look at your boobs.
jokes.setup: Jack's girlfriend Elisa returns; he greets her warmly then immediately
jokes.punchline: 'My God. Look at your boobs.' — Jack's romantic reunion is immediately derailed by a very specific physical observation, delivered with what appears to be genuine awe rather than sleaze
jokes.explanation: Gets a laugh mostly from the timing and Jack's delivery. The joke is in how quickly the tender reunion pivot happens. Decent character beat but relies more on the actor than the writing.

jokes.text: # The rainbows and the cobwebs and the cobwebs and the rainbows... / And stop.
jokes.setup: Becca and Tim are reunited; they celebrate somehow
jokes.punchline: 'And stop.' — Someone cuts off Becca's terrible song with the same dismissive command Liz used earlier, and now Liz herself has adopted it
jokes.explanation: The song callback works because the lyrics have gotten even more circular ('cobwebs and the cobwebs and the rainbows') and 'And stop' is now a running catchphrase for ending bad music. Economy is excellent — two words close the entire music subplot.

jokes.text: I guess, in a way... we both lost children today. Yeah, but mine was real, Jack. Yours was Frank.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz reflect on the day's events — Liz losing Becca's baby, Jack losing Frank
jokes.punchline: 'Yours was Frank.' — Liz punctures Jack's attempt at emotional equivalence by noting that Jack's 'child' was a 35-year-old comedy writer named Frank
jokes.explanation: Excellent button for the episode's emotional throughline. Jack's grandiose framing ('we both lost children today') is demolished by Liz's four-word correction: 'Yours was Frank.' The deadpan delivery and the bathos of naming Frank specifically is perfect. Economy score is high because maximum deflation is achieved in minimum words.

jokes.text: Don't worry, Lemon. I'm confident that someday you'll have... everything you want. Can someone please tell me how to get out of this building? It's like a maze! I keep walking past the same... Sbarro's!
jokes.setup: Jack delivers a heartfelt closing line to Liz; the moment is punctuated by Tim wandering out lost
jokes.punchline: Tim — the young man who just had a transformative emotional experience — can't find his way out of 30 Rock and is lost by a Sbarro's; 'Sbarro's' as a specific detail inside 30 Rock is the absurdist anchor
jokes.explanation: The emotional swell of Jack's heartfelt line is instantly deflated by Tim's confused wandering and 'Sbarro's!' The specificity of Sbarro (a budget mall pizza chain inside a TV studio) is perfectly absurd. It also undercuts Tim's dramatic growth moment by revealing he can't navigate the building.

jokes.text: Can someone please tell me how to get out of this building? It's like a maze! I keep walking past the same... Sbarro's!
jokes.setup: The touching final scene is interrupted by Tim wandering in, lost in 30 Rock
jokes.punchline: 'I keep walking past the same... Sbarro's' — the specific detail that 30 Rock contains a recurring Sbarro, which is both absurd and plausible for a large midtown building
jokes.explanation: A great comedy button — the sincere emotional scene is punctured by Tim's pratfall entrance. 'The same Sbarro's' is the specific detail that makes it land: a maze of Sbarro locations is somehow both absurd and credible for 30 Rock's building.

jokes.text: Yeah. I'm a celebrity! Please! Sad.
jokes.setup: Tim is still lost in 30 Rock, now apparently invoking his non-existent celebrity status to get help
jokes.punchline: Liz's one-word epitaph: 'Sad.' — a perfect, complete dismissal of Tim's attempt to use celebrity privilege he doesn't have
jokes.explanation: Liz's 'Sad.' as a one-word episode button is economically perfect. It simultaneously closes Tim's arc (his delusion about his own status), closes Liz's arc (she's letting go), and gets a laugh. Economy score is 10 — one word does all of this work.

tmdb_overview: Liz befriends a pregnant teenager from a donut shop she visits in the hopes to adopt her baby. Kenneth plans a combined birthday party for Tracy and Jenna, but Jenna wants all of the attention and a party of her own. Jack agrees to go out and party with Frank to keep his mind off of his absent girlfriend and ends up bonding with him over their parental issues.
insight: Tracy's exit arc generates 59 jokes in 42 minutes—a 2.82/min density powered by character absurdism.
